turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, take a seat there. What's brought you?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this rash, and I want the whole story out because I've been turning it over since Tuesday. It started on the insides of both forearms, mad itchy, and then a bit showed on my neck. I cannot tell if it was something I ate, or the new cream, or the antibiotic, and I've gone round in circles.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll take them one at a time. Tuesday, so you're having it about three days?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days, yes. Tuesday evening I was on the couch and I started clawing at my arms. By Wednesday it was red and bumpy, and this morning it's still there, a small bit angrier if I'm honest.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'd say the same. I've been in the house with her and she's been scratching since Tuesday, worse after the telly goes off.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the itch worse at night, then?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Desperate at night. In the day I can nearly park it if I'm busy on the desk at the library, but in bed I'm wrecked from it. I was up at two and again at four, just standing in the kitchen letting my arms cool.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She put a damp tea towel on them at one stage. I told her that wouldn't do much.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It did nothing, you're right. And a hot shower yesterday made it flare, which annoyed me, because I only got in thinking the water would soothe it.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the lips or the tongue, or trouble getting a breath?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No swelling, no tightness, nothing like that. I kept checking the bathroom mirror in case it went that way, and it hasn't, not even a tingle.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): And a temperature, or feeling unwell in yourself?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I feel grand apart from being tired from the not sleeping. I dug the thermometer out of the press and it looked normal, but I didn't write the figure down, so I won't invent one for you.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't, sure. Tell me about the antibiotic, that's the piece I'd be most wary of.

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Flucloxacillin, five hundred milligrams, four times a day, by mouth, started by my GP in Rathmines last Friday for a cut on my left index finger. I nicked it on a tin in the press and it went mucky and hot, and I have taken every dose. It's day five, with two days left in the box, and the finger is settling, less red than it was.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been good with them. I leave the capsule by her breakfast and her tea so none get missed. The midday one she takes herself at the library.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): The midday one is awkward, I have to take it with a swallow of water in the staff room, and someone always asks what it's for. I tell them it's a finger, not anything catching, which it isn't.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the new cream. What exactly did you buy?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Aveeno, the daily moisturising cream in the pump bottle, from the chemist about ten days ago, for hands that were dry from the washing-up and the library heating. I put it on morning and night, hands and up the forearms, and I never stopped, because I thought a moisturiser couldn't do this. The rash sits mostly where I rub it, though I did put a bit on my neck on Monday because it was dry there, and now the neck is in on it too.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She was putting it on thick, I thought. Great lumps of it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): It was not lumps. A normal amount, maybe a bit more than a pea, but not handfuls. I don't want that written down wrong or I'll look like I bathed in it.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Normal amount, grand. And the food, what are you pinning that worry on?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Sunday my sister brought garlic prawns and I had a proper plate, more than I'd usually take, though I've eaten prawns loads of times with no bother. There was a lemon yogurt I don't usually buy as well, only two spoonfuls, so I doubt that one. Prawns were Sunday and the rash was Tuesday, so there's a gap, which is half the reason I can't swear to any of it.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was there anything else new, a washing powder, or a different soap?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No, same washing powder we've had for years, and the same soap. I did think of that in the middle of the night and I checked the press, and nothing was new except the Aveeno. I even sniffed the powder like an eejit and it smelt the same.

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): So prawns on Sunday, Aveeno about ten days, fluclox since Friday, rash since Tuesday. I'm saying this out loud so you can hear me think: it could be contact from the cream, it could be the flucloxacillin, or it could be the prawns. I'm not pinning it on one of them, and I will not put a diagnosis down today.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That's all I wanted, because if you said definitely the prawns I'd argue, and if you said definitely the tablet I'd argue as well. I just need the itch to ease off so I can sleep.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies you know of? Tablets, food, plasters, anything.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none at all. I've always said no known allergies on every form, and I had penicillin years ago for a chest infection and I was grand. I think I had amoxicillin too when I got the wisdom tooth out, and there was no rash that time either.

[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's not what her mother told me. Her mother said the very same blotchy rash came up when she was a child, after penicillin, and they were told to steer clear of penicillin after that. I've heard it more than once since I've been living in.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother mixes up every illness in the family. I did not have a penicillin allergy, and if I had I wouldn't be on flucloxacillin this week taking every dose and grand with it. She's remembering measles, or a heat rash from a caravan in Wexford, and I am telling you no.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. You don't accept that history, and your carer has a different account that came from your mother. I'll write down both, and I am not treating it as a confirmed penicillin allergy.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I don't want a false allergy stuck on the file, because then they won't give me a penicillin, and people say the other antibiotics wreck your stomach. I haven't actually had those, I'm only repeating what the chemist said once.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair. Let me have a look at the skin. Both forearms are red and a bit raised, blotchy, no blisters, and the skin isn't broken. The neck is the same pattern but lighter, there's nothing on the face, and the cut on the left index finger looks clean and isn't hot.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): The neck is itchier than it looks, if that makes any sense, and the right forearm is worse than the left. That's odd, because I'm left-handed and I'd have thought I rubbed more cream on with the left, unless I did the right arm first. I'm overthinking it again.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): You might be. Looking at it doesn't let me separate cream from drug from food, which is why I'm not naming one.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's barely slept two nights. If there's something for the itch, make it a non-drowsy one, because she has an early shift and I don't want her dozing on the bus.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): The bus is grand, I won't doze, but yes, non-drowsy if you can. I tried a cold flannel and it was useless. I nearly bought Piriton and then didn't, because it knocks me out, which I remember from a hay fever year.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold the Piriton so. I was going to send you for patch testing to the Aveeno and let you finish the two days of fluclox, seeing as the finger is nearly there.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd rather finish the fluclox, if I'm honest, because the leaflet is very strict about the full course. I don't want the finger flaring the week I'm back on the early desk. Two days feels stupid to throw out.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And I'm only saying it again because it matters. If her mother is even half right about the penicillin, finishing that box is the bit that worries me.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's what changes it for me. Even with the story disputed, I'm not happy leaving you on flucloxacillin, so stop it today and don't take this evening's dose. And I am not booking a patch test now.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop it altogether, with two days sitting in the box? I want to be sure I heard that. And the Aveeno, do I keep that or bin it, because there's half a bottle and it wasn't cheap at all.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the Aveeno as well until the rash has gone, so both of them are off. What I will start is cetirizine, ten milligrams, once a day, by mouth, for the itch, and it's non-drowsy for most people. Start this evening.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Cetirizine, ten milligrams, once a day. Do I get that from you on a script, or do I just pick it up, and for how long? I don't want to be on a tablet for months over a rash that might be gone by the weekend.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll prescribe two weeks, and if you're well before that you can stop it. If the rash hasn't settled in a fortnight, then we can talk about patch testing, but only if it hasn't settled, not today.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And if the finger goes mucky again with no antibiotic on board, what do we do? I don't want to be guessing at the weekend.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it turns hot or starts weeping, come back and we'll choose something that isn't a penicillin. I'm not starting a replacement now, because it looks quiet.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): So no new tablet for the finger unless it acts up. What about the prawns, am I avoiding those for life, because my sister will make a drama and it might not even have been them?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't ban them for life on a maybe. Leave them off until the rash is gone, and after that it's up to you, because I'm still not saying they did it.

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Leave them for now, not forever, and I'll tell her. She'll argue, but that's between ourselves. The parking outside was a nightmare as well, and I was half afraid the rash would be gone before I found a space, which it wasn't.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come straight back if your lips swell, or your breathing goes, or the rash starts to blister. Don't sit on that until the two weeks are up.

[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Lips, breathing, blisters, straight back. Otherwise am I just to ring, or have you an actual time in mind? I like a time, otherwise I'll put it off and then turn up in a panic.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you here in two weeks regardless, so we can look at whatever is left of the rash. Reception will book it on the way out.

[SEG0055] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll see she takes the cetirizine this evening, and the fluclox goes back in the press and stays there. Will I bring the Aveeno in next time, in case you want the ingredients off the bottle?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the bottle only if the rash is still there and we're talking patch tests, and if it's gone leave it at home. Don't start any other new cream while this is settling.

[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): No new creams, bottle only if it's not gone, cetirizine tonight, fluclox stopped. I might still write it on the back of an envelope when I get in, because I'll convince myself fortnight means something else, even though I know it doesn't.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fortnight is two weeks, the same visit. You're fine to head once the desk has you booked.

[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): One more thing, and tell me if it's nonsense. The lemon yogurt, even two spoonfuls, should I leave that out as well, or am I being ridiculous because the pot is still in the fridge staring at me?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two spoonfuls and a gap, I wouldn't chase the yogurt, so finish it or bin it, I don't mind. It isn't part of the plan.
[SEG0061] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll bin it, she's happier when the maybe-foods are out of the house. And I'll ring the surgery only if the finger weeps, not for every scratch.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ring if the finger weeps or those warning signs show, yes. Otherwise I'll see the two of you in two weeks, so mind yourselves on the way out.

omissions.text: Patient reported no tongue swelling and no throat/chest tightness, and said there had not even been a tingle.
Patient felt otherwise well apart from tiredness due to poor sleep from itching; home thermometer was normal though no exact value was recorded.
Flucloxacillin course details were more specific: started last Friday by GP in Rathmines, on day 5 with 2 days left, and patient had taken every dose.
Aveeno cream application sites were hands and up the forearms, with some applied to the neck on Monday; the rash was mostly where the cream was rubbed on.
Potential food exposure included garlic prawns eaten Sunday in a larger-than-usual amount, but patient had eaten prawns many times previously without problems.
Possible lemon yogurt exposure was discussed: patient had only two spoonfuls of a new lemon yogurt and doctor said not to chase the yogurt as part of the plan.
Patient specifically reported previous amoxicillin exposure after wisdom tooth extraction without any rash.

Doctor documented that the patient does not accept the childhood penicillin-allergy history from the mother, caregiver gave a conflicting account via the mother, and doctor would write down both while not treating it as a confirmed penicillin allergy.
Exam detail missing: the neck rash had the same pattern as the forearms but was lighter.
Patient added that the neck was itchier than it looked and the right forearm was worse than the left.
Patient had nearly bought Piriton but did not take it because it had previously made her very drowsy during a hay fever episode.

Doctor first considered letting her finish the remaining flucloxacillin and sending for patch testing, but changed plan after the caregiver re-raised the possible penicillin allergy; patch testing was explicitly not booked now.
If the finger becomes hot or starts weeping, the plan was to come back and choose an antibiotic that is not a penicillin; no replacement antibiotic was started because the finger looked quiet.
Red-flag advice also included coming back straight away if the rash starts to blister, not just if lips swell or breathing worsens.
